q-84490.name: Question 1
q-84490.problem: A fair six-sided die is rolled $7$ times. What is the mean of the number of times that the outcome of a single roll is a $2$ or a $3?$
q-84490.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times a $2$ or $3$ is rolled.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=7$ rolls

- the probability of getting a $2$ or $3$ on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(7,\frac{1}{3}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the mean is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the mean number of times we get a $2$ or a $3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =7\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130755.name: Question 2
q-130755.problem: A fair coin is tossed $20$ times. What is the mean number of tails that occur?
q-130755.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of tails that occur. 

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=20$ tosses

- since the coin is fair, the probability of landing on tails for each toss is $p=\frac{1}{2}$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(20,\frac{1}{2}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the mean is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the mean number of tails that occur is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =(20)(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p),
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =25\cdot \frac{1}{4}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =25\cdot \frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{75}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130883.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of students having the flu next week.

Here, we have the following information:

- the probability of selecting a student having the flu next week is $0.2$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(23,0.2).$ 

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of students having the flu next week is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{np(1-p)} \\  & =\sqrt{(23)(0.2)(1-0.2)} \\  & =\sqrt{(23)(0.2)(0.8)} \\  & =\sqrt{3.68} \\  & ≈1.918\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
